title: Sefa family tries to make sense of tragedy
article: Whatever Haki Sefa was thinking in the hours and days leading up to the fatal stand-off with Winnipeg police on Highway 59 last weekend, he knew he wouldn't see his children again. The 44-year-old journeyman plumber, who was shot by police Sept. 20, left each of his four children goodbye letters, including one to his 11-year-old son Taib, telling him that "daddy's in a better place now," according to Sefa's wife Lisa Sefa.
"I just wish there was something that we could have done for Haki," Lisa told the Winnipeg Sun. "If he was hurting, I wish he could have reached out to us."
A family member - Lisa believes it was Haki's brother - called police Sunday after they discovered the goodbye letters and were worried about what Haki might do next.
After she was told about the letters, Lisa and Taib drove to her sister-in-law's in the city but spotted her husband travelling northbound in his white van on Highway 59 with police in pursuit.

"I passed him and then I spun around and started chasing them and my son was trying to get in touch with him on the phone, my youngest son, my eleven year old," said Lisa. "By the time I caught up to them it was maybe a minute and they had already blocked it off and I'm pretty sure they had already shot Haki."
Lisa says she hasn't read the goodbye letters yet, three of which went to their adult children aged 20, 22 and 24.
But Taib did share the contents of his note with his mom.
"My youngest son read his letter," said Lisa. "He just vaguely said mom, daddy's proud of me and (to) continue with sports and (he) loves me and daddy's in a better place now."
Lisa said she doesn't know how much her husband suffered from depression. They hadn't lived together for several years but maintained close contact for the sake of their children.
"We still parented our kids together, even though we were separated," she said. "The important thing for us was our children."
She also didn't know how much the recent death of their niece Breanna - who Lisa and Haki helped raise - played a role in what happened last week, but it may have pushed him over the edge.
If he was suffering from depression, like many who struggle with the mental illness, he didn't show it.
"He was always trying to be so strong for everybody else," said Lisa. "He was a good man, he loved his children - they loved their dad."
A friend of Lisa's did see Haki on the Saturday prior to the shooting and told Lisa "he looked sad."
"I tried calling him and texting him but he wouldn't answer," said Lisa.
Sadly, she would never see him again.
Lisa doesn't blame police or anyone else for Haki's death because she doesn't know what happened.

What she can't understand, though, is why no one from the province's Independent Investigation Unit has contacted her yet. She left police her name and number when she arrived on the scene but still hasn't heard from authorities.

You'd think the IIU, which took over the case within hours of the shooting, would want to speak to family to get as much information as possible about the case, especially when they just put out a release Friday asking people to call if they had information.
Whatever the case, our hearts go out to Lisa, her kids and her family.
This was a terrible and entirely avoidable tragedy.
